problem: Map-based training-free VLN methods accumulate broad (dense) semantic annotations of the scene, which costs perception computation and clutters the visual-spatial map given to the VLM planner, without necessarily improving the navigation decision.
motivation: Instructions already name the few landmarks relevant to each decision (e.g. couches and kitchen counter), so grounding every visible object is wasteful and may add noisy detections. The paper asks whether persistent geometry plus sparse, instruction-driven semantics is enough for good instruction following.
key_idea: Persist a lightweight geometric BEV map, but invoke open-vocabulary segmentation only for the landmark queried by the active sub-instruction, and only when the VLM judges it visible and metrically useful, storing results in sparse landmark memory for VLM waypoint selection.
insight: The semantic-strategy ablation shows that both scope and schedule matter: dense+continuous 36.7 SR, dense+on-demand 38.8, instruction-related+continuous 40.2, instruction-related+on-demand 42.8 (all above no-semantics 34.6). Accurate metric grounding matters (segmentation localization 0.12 m error, 42.8 SR vs box 0.51 m, 40.2 SR vs VLM-only 1.56 m, 34.6 SR). Agent-centered heading-up BEV and hybrid frontier+local candidates also give large gains. The authors caution that the gains cannot be attributed purely to reduced clutter.
method: Geometry-centric BEV memory: RGB-D/range points between z_min and z_max rasterized into an obstacle map, then dilated, morphologically closed and inflated by robot radius (0.1 m); rendered agent-centered and heading-up for the VLM.

Hybrid waypoint proposals: frontier candidates (clustered navigable cells adjacent to unknown space) plus local directional candidates (left/front/right offsets at distance d_l) with collision checks.

Hierarchical instruction manager: decomposes the instruction into ordered sub-instructions, tracks completed/current/upcoming items, advances on completion, and extracts the active landmark query (possibly multiple labels, possibly the upcoming landmark).
Semantic trigger: VLM takes observation, history, sub-instruction and query and outputs visibility scores and a grounding decision; a temporal cooldown suppresses redundant calls.

Open-vocabulary segmentation and 2D-to-3D projection: SAM 3 with the landmark text prompt; masks are back-projected with depth, outlier-filtered, clustered, and stored as (label, center) instances in sparse memory M^S.

Landmark-conditioned candidate selection: GPT-5 receives BEV with geometry, landmarks and candidate IDs, recent frames, sub-instruction and progress, then picks a candidate; A* plans on the inflated map.

setting.backbone: GPT-5 (frozen) as VLM planner/trigger, SAM 3 for segmentation
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D with odometry (LiDAR-based localization on the real robot)
setting.action_space: selected frontier/local waypoint candidates executed by an A* path planner (low-level continuous motion)

numbers_note: Paper does not state whether the full val-unseen split or a subset was used; assumed full. Ablation tables report SR only (some on R2R-CE, instruction/memory on RxR-CE).
results: SparseNav reaches 42.8 SR / 35.2 SPL on R2R-CE and 40.7 SR / 24.1 SPL on RxR-CE val-unseen, beating zero-shot baselines such as DreamNav (32.8 SR), InstructNav (31.0) and CA-Nav (25.3), and exceeding supervised NaVid and MapNav in SR. It still trails ETPNav (57.0/54.8 SR) and Dynam3D on R2R-CE.
limitations: Rule-based candidate generator restricts the VLM to predefined frontier/local waypoints that may omit better route waypoints.
VLM (GPT-5) inference is the computational bottleneck in the sequential perception-reasoning-execution loop, delaying motion.
SR remains below navigation-trained methods; cross-paper comparisons are not controlled; real-robot results are qualitative only with no quantitative metrics.
